summary: Defines an optional Content-MD5 header field, a message integrity check that lets the receiver verify the decoded data is the same data that was sent. It was replaced by RFC 1864.

plainLanguage.summary: The optional Content-MD5 field lets a recipient compare a digest of decoded MIME data with one made by the sender. It is intended to detect accidental changes, and RFC 1544 was later replaced by RFC 1864.

questions: how to verify email message integrity
what does the content-md5 header do
how is the content-md5 value calculated
subtitle: An optional MIME header for checking that decoded content was not accidentally changed

tldr.problem: MIME data may be damaged during email transport, so a recipient needs a way to check whether decoded data matches what was sent.
tldr.mechanism: The originating user agent computes an MD5 digest over canonical raw data, encodes it with base64, and puts it in the optional Content-MD5 field.
tldr.outcome: The field checks integrity against accidental modification; RFC 1544 was later replaced by RFC 1864.

sections.title: An Optional Integrity Check
sections.content:
MIME provides mechanisms intended to protect data during email transport, but the RFC says a separate check is still desirable to verify that decoded data remain intact. Content-MD5 is an optional header field used as a message integrity check.

MD5 produces a 128-bit digest of data. The RFC says changes to the data are expected to be reflected in changes to the digest with a high degree of confidence.
sections.plainLanguage: The header contains a digest that the receiver can check after decoding the MIME data. A different digest indicates that the data changed.

sections.title: Generating and Encoding the Digest
sections.content:
Only the originating user agent generates Content-MD5; relays and gateways are forbidden from generating it. The sender computes MD5 over the canonical form of the raw data before applying a content-transfer-encoding. For text, each newline is represented as a carriage-return/line-feed pair.

The 128-bit digest is viewed as 16 octets in network byte order and encoded with base64 for the header value. Because adding or removing trailing white space changes the digest, the RFC says quoted-printable or base64 should be used as the content-transfer-encoding when Content-MD5 is present.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender calculates the digest before encoding the data for transport. It then converts the digest into base64 text and places that value in the header.

sections.title: Checking the Field and Its Limits
sections.content:
If Content-MD5 is present, a recipient user agent may undo the content-transfer-encoding and calculate the digest to check whether the MIME entity changed during transport. A gateway may remove the field if it translates the entity into a different content type, but relays and gateways must not alter processing because the field is present.

The RFC describes this as protection against accidental modification. It contrasts the field with a secure integrity service, such as the one provided by Privacy-Enhanced Mail.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver can recalculate the digest and compare it with the header. The RFC describes this as a check against accidental changes, not as the secure integrity service provided by PEM.
